books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Booker T. Washington, Up From Slavery: An Autobiography (1901), Chapter 1

stimulus.text:
“…some man who seemed to be a stranger (a United States officer, I presume) made a little speech and then read a rather long paper—the Emancipation Proclamation, I think. After the reading we were told that we were all free, and could go when and where we pleased. My mother, who was standing by my side, leaned over and kissed her children, while tears of joy ran down her cheeks. She explained to us what it all meant, that this was the day for which she had been so long praying, but fearing that she would never live to see.”

—Booker T. Washington, Up From Slavery: An Autobiography (1901), Chapter 1
stimulus.source_note: Booker T. Washington, Up From Slavery: An Autobiography (1901), Chapter 1, “A Slave Among Slaves.” Public domain (Project Gutenberg eBook #2376). Wording verified against the Gutenberg text; the excerpt begins mid-sentence, marked with a leading ellipsis.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Washington wrote his memoir in 1901, looking back on the day of emancipation. Which of the following best explains why his memory of joy and the later history of Reconstruction can both be true?

options.text: The Emancipation Proclamation freed enslaved people in every state at once.
options.misconception: Background: the Proclamation applied only to Confederate-held territory, not to the border states.

options.text: The Thirteenth Amendment was ratified before the Proclamation was read.
options.misconception: Background: the amendment came in December 1865, after the Proclamation of January 1863.

options.text: Washington’s family left Virginia for Kansas in 1879.
options.misconception: Background: Washington went to Hampton Institute in Virginia, not to Kansas with the Exodusters.

options.text: Emancipation ended slavery, but not the question of what freedom would mean.

rationales.A: Background: the Proclamation applied only to Confederate-held territory, not to the border states.
rationales.B: Background: the Thirteenth Amendment came in December 1865, after the Proclamation of January 1863.
rationales.C: Background: Washington went to Hampton Institute in Virginia, not to Kansas with the Exodusters.
rationales.D: The joy was real: slavery was over and the family was free. But freedom’s meaning — land, wages, voting, safety — was still fought over for decades, so a joyful memory and a hard history fit together.
rationales.general:
1. Washington’s joy is about one day: the day his family learned they were free.
2. Background: the decades after that day decided what freedom would mean in work, voting, and safety.
3. Those decades brought sharecropping, violence, and laws that narrowed Black rights.
4. A true memory of joy and a true history of limits describe two different things.
Remember: an event can be real and wonderful while its promise stays unfinished.
